source.title: Identifying Interpretable Subspaces in Image Representations
source.authors: N. Kalibhat; S. Bhardwaj; C. Bruss; Hamed Firooz; Maziar Sanjabi; S. Feizi

record.tranche_reason: The study examines highly activating image sets for individual representation features using FALCON, a different method from the original circuit visualizations, and reports whether those sets appear to share interpretable concepts.
record.gate_note: The study reports qualitative examples of individual features activating diverse image sets, and of joint feature activations producing more coherent sets. It does not report a quantified prevalence of polysemantic neurons. The reported percentages of features with more than 10 highly activating samples are not measures of polysemanticity. Human evaluations of concept relevance, method comparisons, and concept-transfer results do not measure the claim's named behavior and are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: It examines top-activating images for individual final-layer features of a vision model (DINO ResNet-50) and reports features firing on visually unrelated images. That bears on V1 by a different method from the original feature visualization. The evidence is qualitative.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. The authors add that fewer than about 20% of final-layer features are explainable individually. Most features activate diverse, unrelated images, while feature groups give coherent, explainable concepts covering more of the representation space.
record.recipe_differences: Uses FALCON: highly activating image crops, CLIP-based captions, and contrastive concept extraction, rather than the original sources' feature visualizations and circuit analyses.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports a difference between individual-feature and joint-feature activation sets: some individual sets are diverse, while selected feature groups produce more coherent sets.

fits_no_version.finding: Images that jointly activate pairs of individually incoherent features form coherent concept sets. The same feature (763) yields different concepts depending on its partner feature.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In vision representations, concepts are encoded by groups of features, and single diffuse features become interpretable in combination.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 202, 2023
record.problems: The examples bearing on V1 are qualitative and limited to selected DINO features; the paper does not quantify how prevalent such individual-feature mixtures are. The authors also note that a strong activation threshold alone does not guarantee an interpretable feature.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows omitted for the 60-row limit. Excluded the feature-activation percentages because they count features meeting an activation-sample threshold, not polysemanticity; excluded human concept-relevance scores because they evaluate FALCON explanations rather than whether a neuron responds to unrelated inputs.

untested.parts: Not tested: InceptionV1 or the canonical cat/car neurons, supervised classifiers beyond a brief mention, and any quantified prevalence of mixed neurons.
No test of capacity or sparsity as cause. Elhage et al. is cited only for the joint-feature observation.
Does not vary activation function or regularization. Per-model threshold percentages (Table A.3) are not polysemanticity rates.
Raises without testing the idea that diverse sets encode abstract concepts.
Does not vary the activation range or the scoring as a test. It only notes that the α threshold alone does not guarantee explainability.

missing.what: General statement that most features activate a diverse image set with no apparent hidden concept, plus additional DINO examples of uncorrelated top-activating sets.
missing.locator: Section 1 (second part); Appendix A.3, Figure A.3

missing.what: Feature pair 1643/2006 shown in Figure 4 (individual sets diverse; joint set is hot air balloons), not recorded.

record.verdict_notes: The study frames diverse-activation features as 'not explainable' or abstract, not explicitly as polysemantic. Linking to V1 is therefore the reader's interpretation, though reasonable. The Table A.3 percentages (e.g. supervised ResNet-50 0.68%, DINO 16.66%) count features with more than 10 samples above a threshold; they are not polysemanticity rates and are correctly excluded. Neither original source is this paper.

versions.untested_parts: Does not examine InceptionV1 neuron 4e:55 or report prevalence across all neurons; examples are from DINO with a ResNet-50 backbone.
No language models or transformer MLP neurons.
Does not test superposition or capacity pressure as a cause.
Does not test initialization, regularization, or training noise as causes.
Does not compare activation functions or regularization, or test whether polysemanticity can be reduced without performance loss.
Does not establish whether the cited canonical mixed neurons have a shared latent feature, or whether truly unrelated mixtures are rare.
Does not vary activation range or explanation-scoring method to measure their effect on polysemanticity judgments.

rows.subject: DINO (ResNet-50 backbone)
rows.operation_detail: Examined images highly activating individual representation features using FALCON.
rows.measure: Whether the highly activating image set appeared to share a human-recognizable concept.
rows.value: The authors describe the image set as diverse, including mushrooms and water towers, with no apparent shared concept.
rows.note: The authors present this as an example of an individual feature whose highly activating images are difficult to explain as a coherent set.
rows.check: Value is right (mushrooms and water towers, Fig. 4). Note the authors read such features as possibly encoding abstract concepts not apparent to humans, not as mixtures. DINO is self-supervised, not a classifier.

relationships.condition: Final-layer features of self-supervised DINO ResNet-50 on ImageNet, at a high activation threshold
relationships.reason: Individual features 188, 1927 and 763 strongly activate visually unrelated image sets (mushrooms/water towers, rockets/morels, fungi/coral), per r1–r3. Figure A.3 shows more such cases. The evidence is qualitative and selected.
relationships.display_finding: Features 188, 1927 and 763 strongly activated on visually unrelated image sets (mushrooms and water towers, rockets and morels, fungi and coral), and the appendix shows more such cases. The examples are qualitative and selected.

tranche.reason: FALCON crop-based concept extraction is a different method on the same question of unrelated top-activating images.

source_check.notes: Qualitative, selected examples. The authors read the diversity as abstract concepts not apparent to humans, not as proven mixtures. The ~20% figure is the share of features with more than 10 images above alpha (Table A.3, garbled: DINO 16.66%, supervised ResNet-50 about 0.68%). The rest are said, without a count, not to activate resembling images. The claim covers supervised models too.

statements.correction: Section 1 claim ('most features activate a diverse set of images', see Fig. 4) is general, with DINO examples. Abstract: fewer than 20% of the representation space is explainable by individual features, in both self-supervised and supervised models. Appendix A.3: supervised ResNet-50 has 'a particularly low number of highly activating features'. Table A.3 (garbled layout) reads about 0.68% for supervised ResNet-50 vs 16.66% for DINO. A.1: supervised ResNet-50 has the fewest interpretable groups (91). So training regime alone does not separate the two studies.
statements.problem: The statement limits this study's 'most features are diverse' claim to DINO and gives supervised vs self-supervised training as the difference between the studies. But the paper makes the claim for supervised models too, including supervised ResNet-50's final layer, which is the same 2048-unit layer 2404.06453 studies.
